ai.definition: Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion (OTEC) is a renewable energy technology that converts thermal energy from the ocean into electricity by utilizing the temperature difference between warm surface water and cold deep ocean water.
ai.howItWorks: OTEC systems typically consist of two main types: closed-cycle and open-cycle. In closed-cycle OTEC, a working fluid with a low boiling point is used to drive a turbine generator. The warm surface water boils the fluid, which then condenses in cold deep seawater, driving the turbine. Open-cycle OTEC uses the ocean water directly as the working fluid, vaporizing it and driving a turbine before returning it to the sea.
ai.problemSolved: OTEC addresses the need for sustainable, low-carbon energy sources by harnessing the consistent temperature gradient in tropical oceans, providing a potentially continuous supply of electricity without emitting greenhouse gases during operation.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process involves designing and constructing OTEC plants, which require specialized equipment and materials. The design must account for the unique environmental conditions at sea, including pressure changes and corrosive effects from saltwater.
ai.buildProcess: OTEC systems are built in stages: initial planning, detailed engineering, construction, testing, and commissioning. Each stage requires careful management to ensure that the system can operate efficiently and safely in marine environments.
ai.costDrivers: Key cost drivers include the high initial investment for plant construction, ongoing maintenance costs, and the need for robust corrosion-resistant materials. Additionally, the remote location of OTEC plants increases transportation and operational expenses.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: OTEC is expected to grow as more projects are developed and technological advancements reduce costs and improve efficiency.
ai.regulation: Regulations vary by country but generally require environmental impact assessments, safety measures, and compliance with local maritime laws. International agreements may also apply, focusing on sustainable use of ocean resources.
ai.risks: Environmental risks include potential impacts on marine ecosystems from thermal discharges and physical structures. Technological risks involve the reliability of the systems in harsh marine environments and the complexity of maintenance.
ai.profitability: Profitability is currently limited due to high initial costs, but as technology improves and more projects are implemented, OTEC could become a viable commercial energy source.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development focuses on reducing costs through improved designs, increasing efficiency, and expanding pilot projects. Innovations in materials science may also enhance the durability of OTEC systems.

glossary.def: A substance used to transfer heat energy from warm water to a turbine in an OTEC system.
An OTEC process where the working fluid is recycled within the system, typically using a low-boiling-point liquid like ammonia or propane.
An OTEC process that uses seawater directly as the working fluid, which is vaporized and then condensed back into water for return to the ocean.
The temperature difference between surface water and deep ocean water used in OTEC systems to generate electricity.

subsystems.name: Cold-water pipe
subsystems.role: draws near-freezing water from 700–1000 m down; the single hardest engineering problem.
parts: suspension or mooring to the platform

subsystems.name: Warm-water intake
subsystems.role: supplies surface water at 25–30 °C in tropical seas.

subsystems.name: Heat exchangers
subsystems.role: transfer heat between seawater and a working fluid with a low boiling point.

subsystems.name: Power loop
subsystems.role: expands vapour through a turbine to make electricity.
parts: working fluid such as ammonia (closed cycle)

subsystems.name: Platform or shore plant
subsystems.role: holds everything together — a moored floating hull, or a land facility on a steep coast.

subsystems.name: Export and co-product systems
subsystems.role: delivers power and, often, fresh water or cold water for other uses.
parts: subsea power cable or onshore substation

buildSteps.title: Find a site
buildSteps.detail: Map where the sea surface is around 25 °C and water near 5 °C lies within a few kilometres of shore at 800–1000 m depth — mostly tropical coasts and islands.

buildSteps.title: Design the cold-water pipe
buildSteps.detail: Size a pipe several metres across for the enormous flow needed, and work out how it survives currents, waves and its own weight.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate heat exchangers
buildSteps.detail: Build large, biofouling-resistant exchangers that keep a tiny temperature difference useful — this is where most of the cost sits.

buildSteps.title: Build the platform
buildSteps.detail: Construct a floating hull or a shore-based plant, plus the mooring system to hold it over the cold-water intake.

buildSteps.title: Install the cold-water pipe
buildSteps.detail: Lower and connect the pipe in one piece or in sections, a delicate offshore operation that has sunk past projects.

buildSteps.title: Assemble the power loop
buildSteps.detail: Fit turbine, generator, pumps and working-fluid charge, and pressure-test the whole circuit.

buildSteps.title: Commission
buildSteps.detail: Start the warm and cold flows together and bring the turbine up to speed, tuning for the small temperature difference.

buildSteps.title: Operate with co-products
buildSteps.detail: Run continuously while making desalinated water, or supplying cold seawater to nearby buildings, to improve the economics.

prerequisites.why: pipes have been deployed, but long-lived, survivable large-diameter cold-water pipes at full scale are unproven.
thermal efficiency is only a few percent, so heat exchangers dominate cost and must resist fouling.
the oil and gas industry already moors and installs large structures in deep water.
floating or shore plants need a reliable connection to the grid.
the resource is fixed by geography — a temperature difference of at least about 20 °C is needed.

pathway.milestone: small pilot plants of tens to a few hundred kilowatts, mainly experimental
pathway.unlocks: operating experience with cold-water pipes and exchangers.

pathway.milestone: 1–10 MW pilot plants combined with desalination or cooling
pathway.unlocks: a revenue stream that partly pays for the very high capital cost.

pathway.milestone: 10–100 MW plants, likely shore-based on island coasts
pathway.unlocks: firm power for tropical islands now running on diesel.

pathway.milestone: large floating plants producing power, fresh water, hydrogen or ammonia
pathway.unlocks: steady baseload energy that does not depend on weather.
